## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Soṇakajātaka* (Ja 529) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection, rendered in English as *Prince Arindama and His Friend Soṇaka*. The canonical commentary sets the introductory framing narrative at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses the assembly on the Perfection of Renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*), observing that he accomplished the Great Renunciation in earlier births as well [Fausböll 1891]. In the narrative of the past, set in Rājagaha, the Bodhisatta was born as King Arindama, whose companion was Soṇaka [Fausböll 1891]. In the Jātaka's conclusion, Soṇaka attains enlightenment as a Paccekabuddha, King Arindama is identified as the Bodhisatta, and his son is identified as the future Prince Rāhula [Fausböll 1891].

Scholarly analysis highlights the narrative's exploration of possessionlessness: it sets the opulence of royal rule against the homeless life of the wanderer, demonstrating the spiritual insufficiency of sovereign power [Fenn 1994]. In the dialogue between the king and the renouncer, poverty is listed among the virtues and blessings of renunciation, serving as a catalyst for the monarch's abdication and adoption of the ascetic life [Fenn 1994].
